Seddon from Imperial College London in the United Kingdom and Stellenbosch University in South Africa, Moorine Sekadde from the National TB and Leprosy Programme in Uganda, Alena Skrahina from the National TB Programme in Belarus, and Rina Triasih from Sardjito Hospital in Indonesia contributed to the development of this operational handbook. 2. The writing, design, and layout of this operational handbook were made possible through funding provided by Unitaid, the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), and the United States Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). 3. The WHO operational handbook on tuberculosis, Module 5, focuses on the management of tuberculosis in children and adolescents. 4. Definitions provided in the handbook are specific to its context and may differ in other settings. For example: Active tuberculosis case-finding involves provider-initiated screening and testing in communities, often using mobile X-ray and rapid molecular tests. Advanced HIV disease in adolescents and children aged 5 years and older is defined as a CD4 cell count below 200 cells/mm³ or a WHO clinical stage 3 or 4 event at presentation for care. All children under 5 years living with HIV are considered to have advanced disease at presentation. Adverse events refer to any untoward medical occurrences during TB treatment with a pharmaceutical product, regardless of a causal relationship with the treatment. Age groups are defined as follows: infants (under 1 year), children (under 10 years), young children (under 5 years), adolescents (10–19 years), young adolescents (10–14 years), older adolescents (15–19 years), and adults (20 years or older). 6. High HIV prevalence settings are defined as those with an HIV prevalence of 1% or higher among adult pregnant women or 5% or higher among people with TB. WHO does not establish thresholds for low, moderate, or high levels of isoniazid resistance prevalence; national TB programs define these for their countries. 7. Bacteriologically confirmed tuberculosis is diagnosed in a biological specimen using WHO-approved rapid tests such as Xpert® MTB/RIF or LF-LAM, smear microscopy, or culture. 8. Contact refers to any person exposed to someone with TB. Contact investigation systematically identifies people with undiagnosed TB disease or infection among the contacts of an index TB patient in the household or similar settings. 9. Decentralization involves providing child and adolescent TB services at lower levels of the health system than where they are currently routinely provided, such as district hospitals, primary health care, or community levels. Interventions include capacity-building for health care workers, expanding diagnostic access, ensuring TB medicine availability, and follow-up care. 10. Differentiated HIV service delivery models simplify HIV service provision to better meet the needs of people living with HIV while reducing unnecessary burdens on the health system. 11. Extensive pulmonary tuberculosis disease is characterized by bilateral cavitary disease or extensive parenchymal damage on chest radiography. In children under 15 years, advanced disease is usually defined by the presence of cavities or bilateral disease on chest X-ray. 12. Family-centered, integrated care models address the needs, values, and preferences of the child or adolescent and their family or caregiver. This includes health education, communication, and psychological support, as well as integration with other child health-related programs and services. 13. Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis strains resistant to at least both rifampicin and isoniazid. Extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB) is MDR/RR-TB resistant to a fluoroquinolone and either bedaquiline or linezolid (or both). 14. Passive case-finding involves patient-initiated pathways to TB diagnosis, where individuals with TB symptoms seek care and are correctly assessed by health workers using diagnostic algorithms. 15. Presumptive tuberculosis refers to individuals presenting with symptoms or signs suggestive of TB.
